title: The Problem of Knowledge and Justified True Belief
text:
Epistemology, the branch of philosophy concerned with knowledge, grapples fundamentally with defining what it means to 'know' something. A traditional formulation posits that knowledge requires three conditions: truth (the proposition must correspond to reality), belief (the knower must believe the proposition), and justification (the knower must have adequate reasons for believing it).

The core philosophical challenge arises in determining whether these three components are always necessary and sufficient. Some theories argue that rigorous justification is the primary hurdle, suggesting that mere truth or belief alone is insufficient grounds for genuine knowledge. Historically, thought experiments such as the Gettier problems illustrated cases where all three conditions appear to be met, yet common intuition suggests that true knowledge is absent.

Modern epistemological inquiry continues to explore alternative frameworks, moving beyond simple justificatory criteria to examine sources of evidence, cognitive reliability, and warranted assertibility in relation to truth.
